issues.subcategory: Real-time framing in the title and abstract
issues.description: Real-time framing in the title and abstract: The title and abstract’s “real time” framing may overstate what the design directly tests. The study uses retrospectively identified historical episodes and does not evaluate prospective monitoring or real-time classification performance, so the wording could lead readers to expect stronger evidence for real-time risk detection than the analyses provide.
issues.quote:
Can Text Messages Identify Suicide Risk in Real Time?
A Within-Subjects Pilot Examination of Temporally-Sensitive Markers of Suicide Risk
Jeffrey J. Glenn1,2,3
Alicia L. Nobles1,4
Laura E. Barnes1
Bethany A. Teachman1
1University of Virginia
2Durham Veterans Affairs Health Care System
3VA Mid-Atlantic Mental Illness Research, Education and Clinical Center (VISN 6 MIRECC)

issues.subcategory: Attempt definition is obscured in the abstract/introduction
issues.description: Attempt definition is obscured in the abstract/introduction: The abstract’s description of the outcome as “suicide attempts” is potentially misleading because the paper later defines attempt episodes to include actual, interrupted, and aborted attempts, including some incidents in which no physical attempt was enacted. Since the distinction between enacted attempts and aborted/interrupted high-intent crises is clinically important, this broader operational definition should be apparent when interpreting the abstract’s main claim.
issues.quote: Objective tools to assess suicide risk are needed to determine when someone is at imminent risk. This pilot laboratory investigation utilized a within-subjects design to identify patterns in text messaging (SMS) unique to high-risk periods preceding suicide attempts. Individuals reporting a history of suicide attempt ( $\mathrm{N}=33$ ) retrospectively identified past attempts and periods of lower risk (e.g., suicide ideation). Language analysis software scored 189,478 text messages to capture three psychological constructs: self-focus, sentiment, and social engagement.

issues.subcategory: Misleading sample size in Abstract
issues.description: Misleading sample size in Abstract: The abstract reports $N=33$ immediately before describing the SMS analysis, but the Results indicate that SMS data were available for 27 participants, and only 15 participants had SMS data for at least one reported suicide attempt. Because the main attempt-versus-lower-risk comparisons depend on the subset with attempt-period SMS data, the abstract may give an inflated impression of the participant-level evidence supporting the core findings.
issues.quote: Individuals reporting a history of suicide attempt ( $\mathrm{N}=33$ ) retrospectively identified past attempts and periods of lower risk (e.g., suicide ideation). Language analysis software scored 189,478 text messages to capture three psychological constructs: self-focus, sentiment, and social engagement.

issues.subcategory: Conflation of variance with AUC/PARP
issues.description: Conflation of variance with AUC/PARP: The $80.3\%$ figure may be mislabeled as variance explained. For a rare binary outcome, this wording sounds like an $R^2$-type statistic and could materially overstate the strength of existing risk-factor models if the source instead reports an AUC, attributable-risk proportion, classification concentration, or another epidemiologic index. The cited metric should be checked and named precisely. As written, the phrase 'accounted for variance' is also difficult to square with the paper’s later emphasis on low base rates and limited acute-risk prediction.
issues.quote: Using data from the World Health Organization, a recent model, which included known risk factors for suicide attempt, accounted for $80.3 \%$ of the variance (Nock, Borges, \& Ono, 2012).

issues.subcategory: Self-report avoidance overstated in study rationale
issues.description: Self-report avoidance overstated in study rationale: The rationale may overstate the degree to which the approach avoids self-report. The communication features are behavioral and archived, but the episode labels and dates defining the risk periods depend on retrospective participant report, so the design relocates rather than eliminates self-report dependence.
issues.quote: Thus, there is an urgent need for novel, data-driven tools to assess acute suicide risk. In light of these challenges, recent work has sought to use behavioral tools to overcome problems associated with self-report. The current study sought to take a similar behavioral approach via a within-person examination of electronic personal communications. This approach helps avoid the complications inherent to either patient or clinician self-report and moves away from traditional between-subjects comparisons, in which many features distinguish people who have versus have not attempted suicide (beyond just suicide attempt status).

issues.subcategory: Base-rate sample-size illustration is off
issues.description: Base-rate sample-size illustration is off: With a 12-month attempt rate of 0.3%, the expected number of attempts in n unselected adults is 0.003n. Thus n = 300 gives 0.9 expected attempts, not one. If the intended statement is about the probability of seeing at least one attempt, the required sample is larger: 1 - (0.997)^300 is about 59%, and a 95% chance would require about 997 people. The low-base-rate point stands, but the numerical illustration should be corrected.
issues.quote: To illustrate the problem, one recent study estimated 12 -month presence of suicide attempt for adults at $0.3 \%$ (Borges et al., 2010), which would mean that at least 300 unselected individuals would be required to produce a single suicide attempt during a one-year follow-up period.

issues.subcategory: Prospective-design claim in low-base-rate rationale
issues.description: Prospective-design claim in low-base-rate rationale: The phrase 'prospective research design' is confusing and methodologically imprecise in this context. The study uses time-stamped messages that precede the attempt windows, but the study recruited participants after relevant events and the attempt episodes themselves were retrospectively identified through interviews; this makes the design better characterized as retrospective use of archival longitudinal data than as prospective follow-up.
issues.quote: Further complicating this problem is the fact that the progression to a suicide attempt (e.g., decision making and planning associated with a suicide attempt) usually begins less than a week prior to the attempt (Millner, Lee, \& Nock, 2016), suggesting the critical period to examine is very narrow. By reconstructing the timeline of recent suicidal behaviors through a retrospective clinical interview, we utilized a prospective research design to understand which features in text communications predicted suicide attempt, overcoming the power issues of a 'true' prospective study design.

issues.subcategory: Claim about studying suicide deaths is too broad
issues.description: Claim about studying suicide deaths is too broad: This is true for designs requiring direct participant report after the event, but it is too broad as a claim about suicide research in general. Suicide deaths can be studied through records, registries, proxy interviews, psychological autopsy designs, and prospective cohorts followed for mortality. Narrow the claim to direct, proximal assessment: many studies that require participant report must rely on non-lethal suicidal thoughts and behaviors, including attempts, as clinically important outcomes.
issues.quote: Second, the problem in suicide research is that the subjects of greatest interest - suicide completers - cannot be directly studied (Millner, Lee, \& Nock, 2015). Therefore, researchers must rely on individuals with non-lethal forms of suicidal thoughts and behaviors.

issues.subcategory: Suicidal ideation is not a form of self-harm
issues.description: Suicidal ideation is not a form of self-harm: This wording classifies suicidal ideation as self-harm. Ideation is a thought or state, while self-harm ordinarily refers to behavior involving injury or intended injury. The next sentence relies on the distinction between suicidal thoughts and suicidal behaviors, so the phrasing should preserve that distinction. “Less severe or more common outcomes, such as suicidal ideation” would make the intended point without the category error.
issues.quote: Due again to low base rates, many studies use less severe forms of self-harm, such as suicide ideation, to serve as outcome measures.

issues.subcategory: Sentiment analysis estimates expressed sentiment, not authorial intent
issues.description: Sentiment analysis estimates expressed sentiment, not authorial intent: “Intended sentiment” is stronger than what these methods observe. Sentiment analysis estimates expressed or text-implied sentiment from linguistic features; it does not verify what the author intended, especially in short interpersonal messages where sarcasm, politeness, and audience effects can change surface meaning. “Estimate expressed sentiment in text” would be more accurate.
issues.quote: For example, the field of sentiment analysis utilizes machine learning and natural language processing to capture an author's intended sentiment (e.g., attitude, opinion, or emotional state) from subjective textual data.

issues.subcategory: Prior-work examples mix prediction with document classification
issues.description: Prior-work examples mix prediction with document classification: The first example fits the preceding discussion of clinical-record prediction. The second is a different task: distinguishing genuine from simulated suicide notes is document classification, not prediction from clinical notes. Separating these examples would make the contrast with the present study cleaner. One option is to say that prior text-analytic studies have included both clinical-record prediction studies and suicide-note classification studies, neither of which directly identifies when a person is at imminent risk.
issues.quote: Key findings include that early childhood abuse reported in clinical records predicts suicide attempts and that computer algorithms are more accurate than clinicians in distinguishing genuine from fake suicide notes.

issues.subcategory: Overbroad claim of novelty across all clinical outcomes
issues.description: Overbroad claim of novelty across all clinical outcomes: The novelty claim may be broader than the paper can comfortably support. The surrounding discussion establishes novelty for private SMS content in suicide-risk research, but the parenthetical 'or any other clinical outcome' is difficult to substantiate and may be vulnerable depending on whether earlier studies using private SMS metadata or related personal communication data are considered within scope.
issues.quote: accumulates automatically and is thus resistant to biases common to the research process, such as demand characteristics or efforts at impression management. This was also the first study, to our knowledge, to collect and analyze private text messaging data for suicide (or any other clinical outcome).

issues.subcategory: Missing theoretical justification for anger
issues.description: Missing theoretical justification for anger: The rationale for anger is less explicit than the rationale for other sentiment features: the introduction motivates negative affect through depressed affect, hopelessness, and anxiety, but the later hypotheses specifically include anger words. Because anger is treated as an a priori sentiment subcategory and becomes an important temporal finding, the theoretical basis for including it is somewhat underdeveloped until the Discussion.
issues.quote: Second, prior research has identified depressed affect (Bulik, Carpenter, Kupfer, \& Frank, 1990), hopelessness (Hawton, Casanas, Haw, \& Saunders, 2013; Smith, Alloy, \& Abramson, 2006), and anxiety (Nock, Deming, et al., 2012) as important risk factors for suicide, suggesting that individuals at suicide risk may use language expressing these emotions at higher rates and with greater negative valence.

issues.subcategory: Unspecified direction of effect in cited literature
issues.description: Unspecified direction of effect in cited literature: The Venek et al. citation is underspecified for the directional sentiment claim. The sentence reports only that positive and negative emotion words were significantly different between suicidal adolescent inpatients and controls, so it does not indicate whether the finding matched the hypothesized pattern of more negative and less positive emotional language.
issues.quote: In support of this idea, use of positive and negative emotion words in transcribed verbal interviews were significantly different among suicidal adolescent inpatients compared to control participants (Venek et al., 2014).

issues.subcategory: Negative sentiment label combines distinct dictionary signals
issues.description: Negative sentiment label combines distinct dictionary signals: In dictionary-based text analysis, more negative-emotion words and fewer positive-emotion words are not algebraic opposites. A message with no positive words is not thereby negative. Death-related content is a separate semantic hypothesis again. The paper would be clearer if it listed these as distinct features: greater negative-emotion word use, lower positive-emotion word use, and greater death-related word use.
issues.quote: In the current study, we tested whether attempt episodes demonstrated significantly greater use of negative emotion words and less use of positive emotion words (as indicators of negative sentiment). We also tested whether attempt episodes involved greater use of words related to the concept of death.

issues.subcategory: Outgoing/incoming message ratios do not measure burdensomeness
issues.description: Outgoing/incoming message ratios do not measure burdensomeness: Counts or ratios of outgoing and incoming messages can speak to communication activity or reciprocity, but they do not measure perceived burdensomeness. The rationale moves from perceived burdensomeness and thwarted belongingness to perceived social support and then to outgoing versus incoming SMS counts, which are related but not interchangeable. The introduction does not fully explain why the sent/received-message ratio should serve as a behavioral proxy for the interpersonal theory constructs. A lower sent/received ratio could mean withdrawal, others reaching out more, or a change in the mix of conversations. The hypothesis should be narrowed to reduced social engagement or altered messaging reciprocity unless the analysis includes content features that capture burden, apology, dependency, support-seeking, or rejection.
issues.quote: In the current study, we tested whether suicide attempters demonstrated greater signs of disengagement from and burdensomeness on their social support networks prior to suicide attempts compared to other episodes by examining patterns in outgoing vs. incoming messages.

issues.subcategory: Directional hypotheses are not tied cleanly to mean versus slope tests
issues.description: Directional hypotheses are not tied cleanly to mean versus slope tests: This sits awkwardly after the directional hypotheses about increased self-focus, more negative affect, and reduced engagement. A slope-only effect is not the same claim as a higher two-week average. For example, a feature could rise from 0 to 14 during an attempt window and still average below an ideation window that is flat at 20. The paper should state that mean differences and within-window slopes are separate exploratory tests, and that a slope effect is evidence of escalation rather than evidence that the whole attempt period had a higher level.
issues.quote: Given the lack of prior research examining when one might expect any differences to emerge prior to a suicide attempt, we did not have hypotheses on whether language differences would be observed for episodes overall (means) but not changes over time (slopes), or vice versa.

issues.subcategory: Screening denominator is ambiguous
issues.description: Screening denominator is ambiguous: This can be read in two ways: the 77 phone screens may be a subset of the 2,377 online screens, or they may be additional people. Those two readings imply different recruitment yields. The main text should specify the flow, for example, “2,377 individuals were screened online, of whom 77 were subsequently screened by phone,” if that is what occurred.
issues.quote: To reach the target recruitment of the lab study, 2,377 individuals were screened online and 77 individuals were screened by phone.

issues.subcategory: Screening criteria systematically exclude non-depressed suicide attempters
issues.description: Screening criteria systematically exclude non-depressed suicide attempters: The participant-pool screening may have narrowed the sampled attempters: respondents were asked about suicide attempts only after endorsing a past period of sadness/hopelessness and willingness to be contacted. Because this criterion is broad and the study also recruited from the community, it does not necessarily exclude all non-depressed attempters, but it may limit generalizability toward people with histories of sadness/hopelessness.
issues.quote: On the participant pool pretest administered at the beginning of the semester (Survey 1), participants were asked, "Have you ever had a period of sadness in the past during which you felt hopeless?" and, if so, they were then asked whether they would like to be contacted about possible participation in studies that ask more questions about this period of time in their life. Those who said yes to both pretest questions were emailed a link to an additional two-question survey (Survey 2), which asked, "Have you ever made a suicide attempt?"

issues.subcategory: Current-risk cutoff is stronger than the label suggests
issues.description: Current-risk cutoff is stronger than the label suggests: On a 0–10 scale, a score of 5 is the midpoint. The protocol may have been clinically reasonable because plan and intent were also excluded, but “minimal or no” does not match a cutoff that includes 5. “No more than moderate current desire to die” would fit the stated rule more closely.
issues.quote: minimal or no current desire to die (i.e., less than or equal to 5 on a $0-10$ Likert scale and no current suicide plan/intent).

issues.subcategory: Current-risk exclusion procedure is not reproducible
issues.description: Current-risk exclusion procedure is not reproducible: The instrument is not named, and the text gives no scoring range, cutoff, or clinical decision rule for “high” versus “imminent” risk. That rule defines who was too acute for participation and is part of the study’s safety protocol. Add the instrument name and the decision criteria used at screening; if final classification was based on clinical judgment rather than a fixed score, say so.
issues.quote: Any participants with intense thoughts of suicide who were determined to be at "high risk" or "imminent risk" for suicidal behavior (as determined by a suicide risk assessment instrument) were excluded from study participation and referred for clinical care.

issues.subcategory: Unclear temporal anchoring in episode identification
issues.description: Unclear temporal anchoring in episode identification: The non-attempt episodes are not temporally anchored as clearly as attempt episodes. Since the slope models code day of episode from -14 to 0, the paper should clarify what day 0 represents for ideation, depressed/high-stress, and positive-mood windows and how those windows were selected; otherwise the temporal trajectories are harder to compare with the two weeks leading up to an attempt.
issues.quote: During the interview, participants were asked to identify a number of specific events or episodes in the past and the calendar dates during which the episodes took place. Episodes included: 1) past actual, interrupted, or aborted suicide attempts, using the two-week period prior to the attempt as a "suicide attempt episode"; 2) two-week episodes of suicide ideation (not resulting in a suicide attempt); 3) two-week episodes of depressed mood or high stress (not resulting in suicide ideation or attempt); and 4) two-week episode of positive mood (i.e., more positive mood than usual and no ideation or attempt).

issues.subcategory: Asymmetric temporal definitions of episodes confound slope analysis
issues.description: Asymmetric temporal definitions of episodes confound slope analysis: The slope comparisons should be interpreted cautiously because attempt windows are anchored to an acute event whereas the comparison windows are lower-risk periods without a clearly comparable endpoint. This asymmetry does not make the interactions trivial, but it means steeper pre-attempt changes may reflect escalation toward an event rather than a feature uniquely distinguishing attempts from other forms of escalating distress.
issues.quote: Episodes included: 1) past actual, interrupted, or aborted suicide attempts, using the two-week period prior to the attempt as a "suicide attempt episode"; 2) two-week episodes of suicide ideation (not resulting in a suicide attempt); 3) two-week episodes of depressed mood or high stress (not resulting in suicide ideation or attempt); and 4) two-week episode of positive mood (i.e., more positive mood than usual and no ideation or attempt).

issues.subcategory: Ambiguous empirical basis for the two-week window
issues.description: Ambiguous empirical basis for the two-week window: The basis for the 14-day window is somewhat ambiguous. The text presents the window as literature-driven and conservative, but then says the optimal window was assessed by visually inspecting the same variables over a wider period. If that inspection informed the chosen window, the slope analyses are more exploratory and data-dependent; if it was only a descriptive check, the phrase "optimal time window" overstates its methodological role.
issues.quote: The decision to set each episode at two weeks long was made in a conservative effort to capture the critical period of increased ideation, planning, and intent leading up to a suicide attempt (Millner et al., 2016). The question of the optimal time window was also assessed empirically, using visual inspection of descriptive figures to identify when the rate of change appeared to be most pronounced. Specifically, temporal visualizations, using a smoother (loess) function, were constructed for each variable of interest and consisted of graphs plotting daily means for the given variable during the 30 days prior to and following the attempt. Although highly variable across variables, changes tended to occur most notably and often around 7 days prior to the suicide attempt.

issues.subcategory: Risk-monitoring item changes names mid-protocol
issues.description: Risk-monitoring item changes names mid-protocol: The paragraph first says participants answered two items: negative mood and desire to die. The trigger for elevated current suicidality then refers to a “desire to hurt self” question, which is not the same construct and was not listed among the two items. If this is the same item, use one label consistently. If a third self-harm item was administered, add it to the item list.
issues.quote: Those who significantly increased in negative affect or suicidality (i.e., any increase of 2 points or greater on the 0 to 10 negative mood and desire to die rating scales) and/or were elevated in current suicidality (i.e., score greater than 3 on desire to hurt self question) were administered a formal suicide risk assessment and assigned a risk level based on their answers.

issues.subcategory: Preliminary analyses sample is inconsistent
issues.description: Preliminary analyses sample is inconsistent: The denominator for the preliminary/descriptive analyses is inconsistent. The methods say demographic, mental-health/suicide-history, and iatrogenic-effect analyses were performed only on participants contributing at least one episode of messaging data, but the Results/Table 1 and iatrogenic tests appear to use all $N=33$, while only 27 participants contributed SMS-containing episodes. The paper should distinguish the enrolled sample from the SMS analytic subsample.
issues.quote:
Preliminary analyses. Preliminary descriptive analyses on demographic information, mental health and suicide history, and other information pertinent to the primary analyses (e.g., iatrogenic effects of the lab study) were performed on the sample of participants contributing at least one episode of messaging data.

Primary analyses. We performed inferential analyses using mixed-effects models to examine within-subject (between-episode) differences among suicide attempters in several communication features.

issues.subcategory: Random-effects specification overstates the final models in Methods and Limitations
issues.description: Random-effects specification overstates the final models in Methods and Limitations: The random-effects description overstates the final temporal-change models. This paragraph says a maximal random-effects model was used, but Primary Analysis 2 later says the full random-slopes structure did not converge and the final model retained only the by-participant slope for episode type. The global model description should not imply that maximal random slopes were used for all primary analyses. This contradiction also affects the Limitations section, where the blanket statement that maximal or near-maximal random effects likely reduced Type I error does not fully fit the Primary Analysis 2 models. Because the central findings are episode type × day interactions, the paper should not rely on the random-effects specification as evidence that those interaction tests were conservative; the Type I-error protection is at best conditional and narrower than stated.
issues.quote: Selection of random effects and specification of models. In line with recommendations by Barr and colleagues (2013), a maximal random effects model, which included random intercepts of participant, episode, and message, and random by-participant slopes, was used to boost generalizability of the findings and protect against inflated Type I error rates. Models were fitted using the "Ime4" package in R (Bates, Maechler, Bolker, \& Walker, 2014; R Core Team, 2013). Generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) used the "glmer" function with a logit link function appropriate for binomially distributed data, which transformed parameters into log-odds units.

issues.subcategory: Binomial model interpretation uses the wrong unit
issues.description: Binomial model interpretation uses the wrong unit: The response described earlier is not whether a message contains at least one LIWC-category word. It is the count of category words versus non-category words within a message. A 10-word message with one anger word and a 10-word message with two anger words both have an anger word “appearing,” but the fitted binomial responses are 1 versus 9 and 2 versus 8. The coefficient therefore concerns the odds that a word token belongs to the LIWC category, not the odds that a text message contains any such word.
issues.quote: For this set of analyses, a significant result says that the odds of a category-specific word appearing in text messages differed as a function of episode type.

issues.subcategory: Likelihood-ratio and Wald tests are conflated
issues.description: Likelihood-ratio and Wald tests are conflated: This sentence names two different tests while describing only one procedure. A likelihood-ratio test compares nested models using the change in log likelihood; a Wald chi-square test uses estimated coefficients and their covariance matrix and does not require fitting the reduced model. Since the next sentence interprets the test as a model-fit comparison, the analysis plan should say “likelihood-ratio tests” unless Wald tests were actually used.
issues.quote: Likelihood-ratio (Wald chi-square) tests were performed to compare goodness of fit for models including and excluding the fixed effect of episode type.

issues.subcategory: Effect-size description conflates coefficient scales
issues.description: Effect-size description conflates coefficient scales: The paper does not describe any standardization step. In a binomial logit model, an lme4 coefficient for a categorical contrast is a log odds ratio; it is not automatically standardized. For LMM outcomes such as message counts, coefficients are in the outcome scale unless the variables were standardized before fitting. Please separate these cases: report GLMM coefficients as log odds ratios, and report LMM coefficients in their measurement units unless standardization was actually performed.
issues.quote: Here, $\beta$ (standardized values of the model parameter estimates in log odds units) are reported and serve as effect sizes.

issues.subcategory: The coded “two-week” window contains fifteen day values
issues.description: The coded “two-week” window contains fifteen day values: The integers from -14 through 0 include 15 day values, since 0 - (-14) + 1 = 15. This matters because the paper repeatedly describes the window as “two weeks” and “14 days leading up to” an attempt, while day 0 may include messages from the attempt day itself. State whether the analysis used 14 pre-attempt days, a 15-day window from -14 through 0, or some other convention, and align the wording throughout.
issues.quote: A series of mixed-effects models were performed for each language feature with 3 fixed effects: episode type ( 4 levels: attempt, ideation, depressed, positive), day of episode (numerical factor ranging from -14 to 0 ), and the interaction of episode type and day.

issues.subcategory: Omission of critical random slopes inflates Type I error
issues.description: Omission of critical random slopes inflates Type I error: The temporal interaction models appear under-specified relative to the stated random-effects rationale. Because the key fixed effect is episode type $\times$ day, dropping by-participant random slopes for day and the interaction after nonconvergence may leave participant-level heterogeneity in temporal trajectories unmodeled, making the tests for slope differences potentially anti-conservative. This choice needs stronger justification or robustness evidence.
issues.quote: The maximal random effects model appropriate for these data included random intercepts of participant, participant-episode, and message, and random by-participant slopes for episode type, day of episode, and episode type by day. Models with the full set of random slopes did not converge; therefore, only a by-participant slope of episode type was included in the final model.

issues.subcategory: Misinterpretation of main effect in interaction model
issues.description: Misinterpretation of main effect in interaction model: The episode-type main effect in the episode-by-day interaction model is not redundant with Primary Analysis 1. If day was entered as a numeric predictor coded from $-14$ to $0$, the episode-type coefficient estimates simple episode-type differences at day $0$, whereas Primary Analysis 1 estimates overall episode-type differences across the observation window. Focusing on slopes is defensible, but the stated reason for disregarding the episode-type main effect is statistically imprecise and may omit a clinically relevant endpoint comparison.
issues.quote: Although episode type and day were included as fixed effects in the models, we were only interested in the interaction term given we evaluated episode type separately already and did not have a theoretical interest in time as an independent variable.

issues.subcategory: Invalid power analysis for mixed-effects models
issues.description: Invalid power analysis for mixed-effects models: The power analysis appears mismatched to the planned mixed-effects models. Cramer's V is not the effect-size metric used for the reported GLMM/LMM fixed-effect tests, and the paragraph does not specify the effective sample size, design effect, degrees of freedom, or assumptions needed to justify using a chi-square approximation for the clustered message-episode-participant data. Furthermore, the cited Cohen’s d values come from between-subject or related-construct literatures, whereas the planned tests are within-subject mixed-effects contrasts, including episode-by-day interactions. The bridge from those prior effect sizes to the assumed large Cramer’s V is not fully specified, especially for the social-engagement measures.
issues.quote: We determined that a sample size of 30 suicide attempters (representing 60 attempts but only 20 with collected, usable SMS data, divided by the design effect) would provide enough power to detect only large effect sizes (Cramer's $\mathrm{V}=0.29$ ) for chi-square tests of mixed-effects models comparing suicide attempts to other types of episodes, assuming $80 \%$ power and a significance level of .05 .

issues.subcategory: Within-subject claim strained in episode characteristics
issues.description: Within-subject claim strained in episode characteristics: Including 12 SMS contributors with no observed suicide-attempt SMS data creates an interpretive ambiguity for the paper's within-subject framing. These participants can inform non-attempt episode estimates, but they cannot contribute direct within-person attempt-versus-non-attempt contrasts, so the primary episode-type comparisons may partly combine within-person and between-person information.
issues.quote: Among the episodes queried during the lab interview, $134(46 \%)$ episodes contained SMS data, collected from 27 different participants. Among these 27 participants, 15 had data from at least one reported suicide attempt; the other 12 participants contributed data from non-suicide attempt episodes and were still included in the analyses. Participants reported and had SMS data for on average approximately 1.5 episodes for each episode type.

issues.subcategory: Episode-average denominator needs to be stated
issues.description: Episode-average denominator needs to be stated: The averages use denominators that are not stated. The 189,478 texts divided by the 134 SMS-available episodes gives 1,414 texts per SMS-available episode, which fits the 1,200–1,600 range; dividing by all 293 queried episodes gives a different value. Likewise, 134 SMS-available episodes across 27 participants and four episode types gives 1.24 participant-by-type episodes, not about 1.5, unless the denominator excludes participants without that episode type. Please specify the denominator for each average.
issues.quote: Participants reported and had SMS data for on average approximately 1.5 episodes for each episode type. Across all episodes, 189,478 text messages were collected and analyzed, ranging between on average about $1,200-1,600$ text messages per episode.

issues.subcategory: Attempt-description denominator is ambiguous
issues.description: Attempt-description denominator is ambiguous: The counts sum to 27, so this appears to refer to all participants with any SMS data. Just above, however, the paper says only 15 participants had SMS data from at least one reported suicide attempt. Since this paragraph describes attempt characteristics, readers may assume the denominator is the 15 with attempt-window SMS. Rephrase as “Among the 27 participants with any SMS data…” if that is the intended denominator.
issues.quote: Among attempters with SMS data, 13 participants reported a single lifetime attempt and 14 reported multiple

issues.subcategory: Attempt method percentages imply non-mutually exclusive categories
issues.description: Attempt method percentages imply non-mutually exclusive categories: For 21 attempts, these rounded percentages correspond to about 9 overdose, 8 hanging/suffocation, and 5 jumping incidents, for 22 method assignments. That is possible if categories were non-mutually exclusive or if some attempts involved multiple methods, but the sentence does not say so. Add “non-mutually exclusive” or specify that multiple methods could be coded for one attempt.
issues.quote: Among the 21 attempts with corresponding SMS data, the most common methods reportedly used or considered/aborted were medications/overdose ( $43 \%$ ), hanging/suffocation ( $38 \%$ ), and jumping from a height $(24 \%)$.

issues.subcategory: Contradictory sign for "Desire to die" change in Table 1
issues.description: Contradictory sign for "Desire to die" change in Table 1: Table 1 appears to have the wrong sign for the “Desire to die (0–10)” pre-to-post change. The text reports a decrease from 0.82 to 0.61, which would be approximately $-0.21$ if calculated as post minus pre; Table 1 lists this value as positive 0.20, while the mood row appears to use the post-minus-pre convention.
issues.quote: latrogenic effects. Examining possible iatrogenic effects of the study, reported mood from pre ( $\mathrm{M}=6.33, \mathrm{SD}=1.38$ ) to post $(\mathrm{M}=6.12, \mathrm{SD}=1.17)$ did not significantly change, $\mathrm{t}(32)=1.05, \mathrm{p}=.304$, and desire to die from pre ( $\mathrm{M}=0.82, \mathrm{SD}=1.10$ ) to post ( $\mathrm{M}=0.61$, $\mathrm{SD}=0.90$ ) significantly decreased slightly, $\mathrm{t}(32)=2.23, \mathrm{p}=.033$.

issues.subcategory: Table 3 contrast labels contradict the text and beta signs
issues.description: Table 3 contrast labels contradict the text and beta signs: The Table 3 pairwise interaction labels appear to be oriented opposite to the reported coefficient signs. Because day is described as ranging from -14 to 0, the reported signs for first-person singular pronouns, positive emotion, and anger seem opposite to an “Attempt minus comparison” reading of the “Attempt vs.” labels. For example, rows labeled “Attempt vs. Ideation” have signs consistent with the contrast being Ideation minus Attempt, which matches the narrative that anger increased more steeply and positive emotion decreased more steeply during attempt episodes. As labeled, however, the coefficients can be read as contradicting the text. The contrast orientation or time coding needs to be made clear enough that the coefficient signs can be interpreted directly.
issues.quote: There was also a significant interaction for anger words, such that anger increased more steeply during attempt compared to all other episode types, including ideation ( $\mathrm{z}=2.00, \mathrm{p}=.046$ ), depressed ( $\mathrm{z}=2.49, \mathrm{p}=.013$ ), and positive ( $z=2.54, p=.0111$ ) episodes (Figure 1C).

issues.subcategory: Discussion overstates mean-difference findings for anxiety and other features
issues.description: Discussion overstates mean-difference findings for anxiety and other features: The opening Discussion appears to overstate the mean-difference findings, an issue that also appears in the Sentiment subsection. Primary Analysis 1 reports a significant episode-type effect only for sad words, while anxiety is explicitly listed among variables with no significant episode-type effect and also does not show a significant episode type × time interaction. The statement that attempt and ideation episodes differed on “a number of language features” also seems unsupported by the reported mean-difference results, which identify only sadness as a significant attempt-versus-ideation comparison. Either report the omitted anxiety contrast, if there was one, or revise the text to clarify that the mean-difference evidence was limited to sadness and was not specific to attempt episodes, unless the anxiety claim is intended as a purely descriptive tendency.
issues.quote:
In terms of overall mean differences, few reliable differences emerged though results indicated that the period of high risk just before a suicide attempt was associated with messages indicating greater anxiety and sadness. However, none of these differences in language use were uniquely associated with suicide attempt episodes, and are therefore not specific characteristics of a high suicide risk state. Although language use was different between attempt and ideation
episodes on a number of language features, such as sadness, these differences did not hold when comparing attempts to other non-suicidal episodes.

issues.subcategory: Interpreting non-significance as similarity
issues.description: Interpreting non-significance as similarity: The discussion of self-focus may slightly overread the non-significant attempt-versus-positive slope contrast ($p=.374$). Because the Results describe positive episodes as flatter and the study is underpowered, the activation/similarity account should be treated only as a speculative interpretation rather than as evidence that attempt and positive-mood self-focus trajectories are genuinely similar.
issues.quote: However, prior research suggests a possible reason why a language variable such as self-focus may behave similarly for attempt and positive episodes despite them being on opposite ends of the risk scale. Agitation and anxiety are better predictors of suicide attempt than a clinical diagnosis of depression (Busch, Fawcett, \& Jacobs, 2003; Nock, Hwang, et al., 2010), which is in line with the thinking that a suicide attempt, in contrast to suicide ideation or depression, is a behavior that requires energy and activation to enact. Accordingly, it is plausible that there are similarities between psychological states during attempt and during positive episodes, which may be reflected by similarities in language use.

issues.subcategory: Self-focus interpretation shifts from activation to suicide risk without support
issues.description: Self-focus interpretation shifts from activation to suicide risk without support: The preceding sentences offer activation as a possible reason why attempt and positive-mood episodes looked similar. That account may be plausible, but it does not support calling the pattern sensitive to suicide-risk level, since positive mood is treated as the low/minimal-risk comparison. A safer interpretation is that first-person pronoun use may reflect activation or arousal rather than suicide risk per se, especially because the text immediately notes that self-focus did not differentiate high risk from all lower-risk states.
issues.quote: This result potentially suggests that self-focus may be especially sensitive to changes in risk related to increased energy or activation, and the "signal" may only be detectable by examining subtle temporal changes.

issues.subcategory: The null death-word result is overinterpreted
issues.description: The null death-word result is overinterpreted: A non-significant death-word effect in a small pilot supports a narrower conclusion: this analysis did not detect episode differences in simple death-related word counts. It does not by itself show that suicide-specific language is unhelpful or that hidden markers are needed. There is also a construct mismatch, since death-related words are not the same as explicit suicidal endorsements; death words can appear in non-suicidal contexts, and suicidal intent can be expressed without a LIWC death term. Additionally, the summary may blur the static and temporal findings, as the Results section does report a significant episode type × time interaction for death words, so stating they “did not significantly differ between episodes” could be read as treating the results as wholly null.
issues.quote: Interestingly, use of death-related words did not significantly differ between episodes, suggesting the need to identify hidden and more subtle signs of risk beyond explicit endorsements of suicide-specific language.

issues.subcategory: LIWC is described as custom while the limitation says it was not tailored
issues.description: LIWC is described as custom while the limitation says it was not tailored: Calling LIWC a “custom dictionary” implies study-specific adaptation, but the next sentence says the categories were not modified for suicide-specific constructs. If the study used the standard LIWC categories, say “predefined LIWC dictionary categories.” If the authors actually customized the dictionary, describe what changed.
issues.quote: In this study, we limited our linguistic analyses to a handful of categories based on the presence of single words in a custom dictionary (LIWC).

issues.subcategory: Machine-learning framing in Future Directions
issues.description: Machine-learning framing in Future Directions: The Future Directions discussion would benefit from more precise machine-learning framing. It moves from unsupervised topic modeling and feature discovery to supervised class prediction, while defining machine learning only in terms of class prediction. Revising the definition to “supervised machine learning” would keep the classifier discussion accurate without excluding the unsupervised methods just mentioned. The claim of 'strong accuracy' also may overstate what is shown by the Kessler risk-concentration statistic alone, since concentration of deaths in a top-risk stratum does not by itself establish clinically strong prediction under a low base rate. For example, in a rare-event setting, if 100 deaths occurred among 100,000 people, placing 5,000 people in the top-risk group and capturing 50 deaths would give a positive predictive value of 1%, while an always-negative classifier would still have very high raw accuracy. Replace the sentence with a metric-aware statement about risk stratification, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and calibration.
issues.quote:
Furthermore, data-driven methods for understanding attempt episodes include unsupervised learning techniques, such as topic modeling, to identify themes in communication prior to suicide attempts that might provide richer descriptions of the themes and inform future predictors of interest. (See Kern et al., 2016 for a useful review of methods for analyzing social media language.) A future study could also examine how language and communication habits change following a suicide attempt, providing potentially valuable insight into the psychological effects of suicidal behaviors. It should be acknowledged, however, that data collection of SMS and other private digital communication is likely to remain an ongoing challenge for researchers, particularly as younger populations transition to closed ecosystems and proprietary platforms (e.g., Snapchat) for their interpersonal communication.

The results of the current study could also serve as the basis for building a machine learning model to automate identification of text features associated with suicide risk. Machine learning refers to a set of algorithms designed to predict membership to a class based on a set of features (James, Witten, Hastie, \& Tibshirani, 2013). Machine learning techniques may be particularly useful for predicting low base rate behaviors like suicide attempts. In a study of Army soldiers, Kessler and colleagues (2015) created a machine learning classifier based on known risk factors and found that $5 \%$ of individuals assigned by the classifier to the highest risk category comprised over $50 \%$ of suicide deaths at follow-up. In another study, Walsh, Ribeiro, and Franklin (2017) used electronic health records to develop machine learning algorithms that predicted future suicide attempts among adult patients. The strong accuracy achieved in these studies demonstrates the ability to use an ensemble of predictors, which on their own would carry trivial predictive value, to predict a complex multifactorial clinical outcome.

issues.subcategory: Misstatement of concentration of risk statistic
issues.description: Misstatement of concentration of risk statistic: The Kessler statistic is compressed in a way that could be read ambiguously. The intended point appears to be that the highest-risk stratum comprised the top $5 \%$ of the sample and accounted for over $50 \%$ of subsequent suicide deaths; as written, the relationship between the $5 \%$ and the highest-risk category is not quite explicit.
issues.quote: In a study of Army soldiers, Kessler and colleagues (2015) created a machine learning classifier based on known risk factors and found that $5 \%$ of individuals assigned by the classifier to the highest risk category comprised over $50 \%$ of suicide deaths at follow-up.

issues.subcategory: Machine-learning paragraph blurs classification targets
issues.description: Machine-learning paragraph blurs classification targets: The machine-learning paragraph does not fully separate the cited classifier's target—attempt/ideation episodes versus depressed mood episodes—from the paper's broader aim of detecting imminent attempt risk. The reported sensitivity and specificity apply to classification of a combined suicide-related episode class, so they should not be read as evidence that the model distinguishes attempts from ideation.
issues.quote:
In a recently published study, our group used a deep neural net machine learning classifier to model within-subject episode type differences between attempt/ideation episodes and depressed mood episodes using an atheoretical set of communication variables (n-grams), including ones
not analyzed in this current study (Nobles et al., 2018). Sensitivity and specificity were moderate to strong, indicating that the algorithm performed fairly well at classifying episodes. These findings suggest the promise of detecting "hidden" but meaningful signals using predictive models, even when only a small number of classification units are available.

issues.subcategory: Retrospective-report limitation is partly undercut
issues.description: Retrospective-report limitation is partly undercut: The retrospective-report limitation partly conflates two validity issues. Although the SMS messages were naturally occurring and less prone to demand characteristics, the temporal analyses still depend on retrospectively recalled episode dates and classifications; inaccurate timing or labeling could misalign the two-week windows and affect the observed slopes.
issues.quote: There are several methodological limitations to acknowledge. First, dates and information regarding episodes relied on retrospective self-report, which may not have been entirely reliable, especially for less recent episodes. A prospective design in which participants were assessed frequently for the presence of suicidal thoughts or behaviors would resolve some concerns about self-report. However, such a design was not practical given the very low base rate of suicide attempts and would necessitate more participants than is feasible for a laboratory study. Further, concerns about this retrospective report are somewhat minimized because, while suicide history was reported retrospectively, the actual communication data used for analyses were not and thus are ecologically valid and not prone to demand characteristics.

issues.subcategory: Multiplicity rationale in Limitations may conflate issues
issues.description: Multiplicity rationale in Limitations may conflate issues: The fifth limitation mixes two distinct Type I-error concerns. The decision to report unadjusted results with caveats is defensible for an exploratory pilot, but the point about maximal or near-maximal random effects concerns the calibration or conservatism of individual mixed-model fixed-effect tests. It does not address the across-outcome multiplicity created by testing many LIWC variables and follow-up contrasts, so the paragraph may over-reassure readers about the many-tests issue.
issues.quote: Fifth, our analyses involved running a fairly large number of tests, which potentially increases the chances of rejecting the null hypothesis due to the sheer number of tests. Given this is a pilot study with a small and already potentially underpowered sample and the fact that we did not have concrete directional hypotheses for many of the tests, we decided not to artificially suppress Type I error (i.e., using a multiple comparisons correction) but rather view any significant results in light of these caveats (Rothman, 1990). Also, using the maximal (or near-maximal) random effects in our models likely decreased the chances of Type I error given prior research that has argued that maximal random effects structures can be overly conservative and lead to a significant loss of power (Matuschek, Kliegl, Vasishth, Baayen, \& Bates, 2017).

issues.subcategory: Conclusion overstates predictive claims
issues.description: Conclusion overstates predictive claims: The conclusion's statement that the study identified novel predictors of suicidal behaviors is stronger than the analyses demonstrate. The data support retrospective within-person associations and temporal markers in two-week windows preceding past attempts, but the paper does not test prospective prediction, out-of-sample classification, calibration, or real-time detection. The future machine-learning language helps, but the predictive claim should be interpreted more cautiously.
issues.quote: The current study utilized a novel, within-subject, laboratory-based research design to identify and better understand real-time patterns in communication unique to periods preceding suicide attempts. This is the first research study, to our knowledge, to examine the association between private text messaging data and mental health outcomes, suicide or otherwise. This laboratory investigation identified novel predictors of suicidal behaviors, which may be utilized in the future by machine learning models to predict acute suicide risk and identify whether and where an individual is on the pathway from thinking about suicide to acting on those thoughts.

The title, abstract, overview, and clinical implications sections heavily position the study around identifying suicide risk in real time. The introduction also states that retrospective timeline reconstruction "utilized a prospective research design." However, the design inherently identifies past episodes after outcomes are known, extracting SMS windows around those retrospectively reported dates to test associations. The clinical force of the manuscript rests on separating this temporal ordering from deployable prediction. Reframing the paper around the strengths of a retrospective within-person pilot study of temporally patterned language will align the claims with the data. Fully prospective real-time prediction, out-of-sample classification, base-rate calibration, and false-positive/false-negative evaluations can then be explicitly reserved for future validation work.

**Data missingness in within-subject contrasts**

The analyses are described in the Methods as within-subject comparisons among suicide attempters. However, the Results section indicates that only 134 of 293 episodes contained SMS data, only 27 participants contributed messaging data, and only 15 had SMS data for at least one attempt episode. Because the other 12 participants contributed only non-attempt episodes but were still included, the fixed-effect contrasts may partly capture between-person differences in data availability rather than purely intrapersonal changes.
